title: Module 9 practice assessment
description: Ungraded practice for Module 9, Particle effects. Take it as often as you like and read the feedback; it is there to teach, not to grade.

questions.prompt: A headless test prints `PASS emitting after hit` for a death burst that is a child of `Player`, and `player.gd` calls `hide()` at the moment of death. What follows?
choices: The burst is visible: `hide()` affects only the node it is called on, so the child keeps drawing while `emitting` is true, and the passing line is reasonable evidence.
It can be emitting yet invisible: a hidden parent hides its children, so the test should also assert `is_visible_in_tree()`, and only a person at a screen confirms it was seen.
It is invisible, but the fix is `visible = true` on the burst itself, since the burst's own visibility flag takes precedence over a hidden parent.
It is visible but misplaced: with `local_coords` false the particles stay where they were born, so the burst plays at the player's spawn point rather than the death spot.
questions.feedback: A particle node inherits its parent's visibility, so a burst under a player that calls `hide()` can be `emitting` and still invisible; a child's own `visible` flag does not override a hidden parent, and `local_coords` only decides whether living particles follow a moving emitter. That is why `DeathBurst` is a child of `Main` and the test asserts `is_visible_in_tree()`; only a person at a screen can confirm it was seen (see "Triggering an effect from gameplay").

questions.prompt: You want sparks that each leave a small puff when they die. Which setup gives that in Godot 4.7.2?
choices: A `CPUParticles2D` whose `sub_emitter` path points at a second `CPUParticles2D`, with `sub_emitter_mode` set to `AT_END`, since the CPU node has near-feature parity with the GPU node.
A `GPUParticles2D` with `trail_enabled` set to true, which spawns a puff behind each spark when it dies, though only outside the Compatibility renderer.
A `GPUParticles2D` whose `ParticleProcessMaterial` sets `sub_emitter_mode` to `AT_START`, with `sub_emitter` pointing at a second `GPUParticles2D` that draws the puff.
A `GPUParticles2D` whose `sub_emitter` path points at a second `GPUParticles2D`, and whose `ParticleProcessMaterial` has `sub_emitter_mode` set to `AT_END`.
questions.feedback: Sub-emitters are a GPU-node feature: the CPU classes have no `sub_emitter` property (checked with `ClassDB` on 4.7.2), and the mode that fires when a particle dies is `AT_END`, set on the `ParticleProcessMaterial`. `trail_enabled` is a different feature, and any other `sub_emitter_mode` picks a different moment (see "Four nodes, two families" and "Beyond the checkboxes, and where the cost lands").

questions.prompt: Codex's cost script printed 6.90 ms per frame for every case, including the empty scene. What is the right reading?
choices: It measured the engine's idle sleep: headless Godot sleeps toward a 6,900 µs frame period unless a fixed frame rate is set, so rerun with `--fixed-fps 60`.
The first frame's delta includes time from before the effect started, so 60 warm-up frames were too few; raising the warm-up to several hundred frames would separate the cases.
The dummy renderer caps every case at one frame period, so the GPU rows are meaningless, but the CPU rows are valid readings and need no rerun.
`Time.get_ticks_usec()` reads wall-clock time while particle time is frame time, so the script should sum each frame's `delta` instead of timing 300 frames.
questions.feedback: An identical number for an empty scene and 50,000 particles means the instrument is wrong, not the particles: any work under 6.9 ms hides inside the idle sleep, so the CPU rows are no more valid than the GPU rows until a fixed frame rate is set. The prompt did not name `--fixed-fps 60`; with it, the CPU cases came out at 0.035, 0.33 and 1.61 ms (see "What the agents got wrong").

questions.prompt: Claude Code said the one failing check was a headless limitation: the dummy renderer never advances particle lifetime timers. Which evidence showed that explanation was wrong?
choices: Running the failing check again with `--fixed-fps 60`, which removes the dummy renderer's idle sleep and so rules the renderer out as the cause.
The agent's own "Expected headless output" table, in which two of three predicted failures did not occur, so its explanation of the third had to be wrong too.
A probe run before any agent: a one-shot `GPUParticles2D` with `lifetime = 0.5` emitted `finished` about 0.5 s after `restart()` in headless Godot 4.7.2.
The 14 passing checks in `test_input.gd`, which include timed spawning, so timers evidently advance headless and particle timers must advance as well.
questions.feedback: A probe run before any agent showed `finished` firing headless, so the fault had to be in the test: a GDScript lambda cannot reassign an outer local variable, so the test read a flag that never changed. The mispredicted table shows the agent was guessing, but not that this explanation was false, and neither `--fixed-fps` nor `test_input.gd` says anything about particle timers (see "What the agents got wrong").

questions.prompt: A death burst passes every state check in `test_particles.gd`. According to the class reference and the official 2D particles demo, which two settings could still leave it as a few specks, some moving along an axis the 2D camera never shows?
choices: A null `texture` (1×1-pixel squares) and `local_coords` left false (living particles stay where they were born instead of following the emitter).
A null `texture` (1×1-pixel squares) and `particle_flag_disable_z` left false (part of each velocity points into Z, an axis a 2D camera never shows).
`particle_flag_disable_z` left false (part of each velocity points into Z) and `fixed_fps` left at its default of 30 (motion updates in visible steps).
An `explosiveness` of 1 with `one_shot` true (all 32 particles are born in the same instant, so they overlap as a few specks).
questions.feedback: With no texture, particles are 1×1-pixel squares, and `ParticleProcessMaterial` is shared with 3D, so without Disable Z part of each velocity points into Z. A state check reads neither, which is why the agent's first burst passed; `local_coords` and `fixed_fps` cause other effects, and `explosiveness = 1` with `one_shot` is exactly what a burst is meant to have (see "Defaults that bite in 2D").

questions.prompt: With `--fixed-fps 60`, 50,000 `GPUParticles2D` cost 0.0024 ms per frame headless and 50,000 `CPUParticles2D` cost 1.61 ms. What may you conclude?
choices: GPU particles are far cheaper than CPU particles, so 50,000 of them are safe on a phone, since 0.0024 ms is well under any frame budget.
The CPU row transfers: 1.61 ms per frame for 50,000 particles is roughly what a phone would pay, because the per-particle price belongs to the node.
The GPU row is real but tiny, the CPU-side cost of submitting 50,000 particles, so only drawing is left unmeasured and fill rate is the one cost to check.
The CPU row is a real simulation cost on the machine that ran it; the GPU row is a dummy renderer doing nothing, so GPU cost needs a real GPU and the Profiler.
questions.feedback: CPU particle nodes simulate on the CPU, so their time shows up in a headless run, but only as a figure for that machine. GPU simulation and drawing do not exist under the dummy renderer, so that row (about the same as an empty scene) is a property of the instrument, not of GPU particles (see "Beyond the checkboxes, and where the cost lands").
